questions.question: During a titration, which piece of glassware should be used to transfer a 25 mL aliquot of a substance to the conical flask?
questions.answer: An aliquot (an accurately known fixed volume) is delivered with a **volumetric pipette** (A). (B) is a burette, (C) a measuring cylinder and (D) a volumetric flask.

questions.question: What is the systematic name for the molecule shown?
questions.answer: The nitrogen carries an ethyl group, a propyl group and a hydrogen, so it is a secondary amine. The longest chain attached to N (propyl) is the parent amine and the ethyl group is the $N$-substituent: $N$-ethylpropanamine ($N$-ethylpropan-1-amine). There is no C=O, so it is not an amide.

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium system:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which set of conditions will produce the highest yield of ammonia?
questions.answer: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right; it also reduces the number of moles of gas (4 → 2), so high pressure shifts it to the right (Le Chatelier's principle).

questions.question: Which of the following is a **position** isomer of pentan-2-one?
questions.answer: A position isomer has the same carbon chain and functional group, with the functional group in a different position. (A) is pentan-3-one. (B) 3-methylbutan-2-one is a chain isomer; (C) cyclopentanol and (D) an enol are not ketones with the same chain.

questions.question: Which analytical technique relies on particles being initially ionised?
questions.answer: In mass spectrometry the sample molecules are first ionised (e.g. by electron bombardment) so that the ions can be accelerated and deflected according to their mass-to-charge ratio.

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium reaction in an aqueous solution:

$$\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + \text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}(aq)$$

At 298 K, the equilibrium constant, $K_{eq}$, for the reaction is 200. A student prepares a solution containing 0.12 mol L$^{-1}$ Fe$^{3+}(aq)$ ions and 0.12 mol L$^{-1}$ SCN$^-(aq)$ ions at equilibrium.

What is the equilibrium concentration of $[\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}(aq)$ at 298 K?
questions.answer: $K_{eq} = \dfrac{[\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}]}{[\text{Fe}^{3+}][\text{SCN}^-]}$, so $[\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}] = 200 \times 0.12 \times 0.12 = 2.88 \approx 2.9$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
HInd is an acid–base indicator used in titration that exists in two equilibrium forms when dissolved in water.

$$\underset{\text{yellow}}{\text{HInd}(aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) + \underset{\text{purple}}{\text{Ind}^-(aq)}$$

Which statement(s) are correct?

i. In a strongly acidic solution, yellow is observed.

ii. When the concentration of HInd$(aq)$ is less than the concentration of Ind$^-(aq)$, yellow is observed.

iii. The concentrations of HInd$(aq)$ and Ind$^-(aq)$ are approximately equal at the end point of a titration.
questions.answer: (i) High $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ shifts the equilibrium left, so yellow HInd dominates — true. (ii) If $[\text{Ind}^-] > [\text{HInd}]$ the solution appears purple — false. (iii) The end point is where the indicator changes colour, i.e. where $[\text{HInd}] \approx [\text{Ind}^-]$ — true.

questions.question: Which organic molecule could have produced this infrared spectrum?
questions.answer: There is a strong, broad absorption centred near 3350 cm$^{-1}$ (alcohol O–H) and no C=O absorption at 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$, which rules out butan-2-one and butanoic acid (whose acid O–H band would also be much broader, 2500–3000 cm$^{-1}$). But-2-ene has no O–H. So the molecule is butan-2-ol.

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium system:

$$2\text{ICl}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{I}_2(s) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \qquad \Delta H = +17\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which of the following changes will increase the chemical amount, in moles, of chlorine that can be produced?
options: Removing some of the solid I$_2$.
Removing the Cl$_2$ gas as it is formed.
questions.answer: $K_{eq} = [\text{Cl}_2]$ — the solids do not appear in the expression, so adding or removing solids does not shift the equilibrium. Removing Cl$_2$ lowers $[\text{Cl}_2]$ below $K_{eq}$, so the system shifts right to produce more Cl$_2$. Decreasing the temperature favours the exothermic (reverse) reaction.

questions.question: Photosynthesis is a highly endothermic reaction. Which of the following is true for the equilibrium constant, $K_{eq}$, at low temperatures?
questions.answer: For a highly endothermic reaction, low temperatures favour the reactants (the reverse, exothermic direction), so very little product is present at equilibrium and $K_{eq} \ll 1$ (but never exactly 0).

questions.question: Which peak would you find in a mass spectrum for propanal but not in a mass spectrum for propan-2-one?
questions.answer: Both have $M = 58$ and can give CH$_3^+$ (15). Propan-2-one, CH$_3$COCH$_3$, fragments to CH$_3$CO$^+$ (43). Propanal, CH$_3$CH$_2$CHO, can lose CHO or C$_2$H$_5$ to give CH$_3$CH$_2^+$ / CHO$^+$ at $m/z = 29$; propan-2-one has no C$_2$H$_5$ or CHO group, so it cannot give 29.

questions.question:
Ibuprofen is a drug used for pain relief. Chemical tests were performed on a sample of ibuprofen and the results of the tests are given below.

| Chemical test | Result with ibuprofen |
|---|---|
| Aqueous sodium carbonate | Effervescence |
| Bromine water | Solution remained orange |
| Acidified potassium permanganate | Solution remained purple |

Which functional group must be present in a molecule of ibuprofen?
questions.answer: Effervescence (CO$_2$) with sodium carbonate shows a carboxylic acid. Bromine water not decolourising rules out C=C, and permanganate not decolourising rules out a primary/secondary alcohol O–H (and C=C).

questions.question: A 0.15 mol L$^{-1}$ sample of hydrofluoric acid, HF, has a pH of 2.00. Calculate the $K_a$ of hydrofluoric acid.
In a glucose fermentation reaction, 1.50 g of ethanol was produced. What volume of carbon dioxide (measured at 25 °C and 100 kPa) was also produced in this reaction?
questions.answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{CO}_2$, so $n(\text{CO}_2) = n(\text{ethanol}) = \dfrac{1.50}{46.068} = 0.03256$ mol. $V = 0.03256 \times 24.79 = 0.807$ L.

questions.question:
Which combination of organic reactant and reaction conditions could be used to produce 2-bromohexane as the sole product in a single step?

| | Organic reactant | Reaction conditions |
|---|---|---|
| (A) | hex-2-ene | Br$_2(l)$, room temperature |
| (B) | hex-2-ene | dilute H$_2$SO$_4(aq)$, heat |
| (C) | hex-3-ene | HBr$(g)$, room temperature |
| (D) | 2-bromohex-3-ene | H$_2(g)$, Pd/C catalyst, heat |
questions.answer: Hydrogenating the C=C of 2-bromohex-3-ene gives only 2-bromohexane. (A) gives 2,3-dibromohexane, (B) gives hexanols, and (C) gives 3-bromohexane.

questions.question: Which statement is true for both ethanol and ethanal? They both produce:
options: A molecular ion peak at $m/z = 46$ in mass spectrometry.
A sharp peak between 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$ in IR spectroscopy.
questions.answer: Each molecule has two carbon environments, so two $^{13}$C NMR peaks. Ethanal has $M = 44$ (not 46), ethanol has no C=O, and ethanol has three $^1$H environments (CH$_3$, CH$_2$, OH).

questions.question:
Aqueous dilution of IO$_4^-$ results in the following reaction:

$$\text{IO}_4^-(aq) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_4\text{IO}_6^-(aq) \qquad K_{eq} = 3.5 \times 10^{-2}$$

50.0 mL of a 0.896 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of KIO$_4(aq)$ is diluted to 250.0 mL with water. How many moles of H$_4$IO$_6^-(aq)$ are present at equilibrium?
questions.answer: Initial $[\text{IO}_4^-] = \dfrac{0.896 \times 0.0500}{0.2500} = 0.1792$ mol L$^{-1}$. Water is omitted from $K_{eq}$: $\dfrac{x}{0.1792 - x} = 0.035 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{0.035 \times 0.1792}{1.035} = 6.06 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$. Moles $= 6.06 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.2500 = 1.51 \times 10^{-3}$ mol. (Option B is the concentration, not the amount.)

questions.question:
A section of the polyester poly(3-hydroxyvalerate) is shown.

A single chain of this polymer is found to have a molar mass of 9530 g mol$^{-1}$ (calculated to 3 significant figures). How many monomer units of 3-hydroxyvaleric acid were required to make a chain with this molar mass?
questions.answer: Monomer 3-hydroxypentanoic acid, C$_5$H$_{10}$O$_3$ ($M = 118.13$). Each condensation releases one water, so the repeating unit is C$_5$H$_8$O$_2$ ($M = 100.12$) and a chain of $n$ units has $M = 100.12n + 18.02$ (one H and one OH at the chain ends). $100.12n + 18.02 = 9530 \Rightarrow n = 95.0$.

questions.question:
Calculate the mass of solid ammonium chloride that must be added to 25.0 mL of water to make a solution with a pH of 4.85.

p$K_a$ of NH$_4^+$ is 9.24. $MM$ of NH$_4$Cl is 53.492 g mol$^{-1}$.

A data logger was used to measure the pH changes during a titration. Hydrochloric acid with a concentration of 0.1024 mol L$^{-1}$ was added to a solution of sodium carbonate that was contaminated with sodium chloride. The titration curve is shown.

The mass and density of the mixture of sodium carbonate and sodium chloride solution aliquot used was 36.98 g and 2.360 g mL$^{-1}$ respectively. What was the concentration of sodium carbonate in the solution?
questions.answer: The first equivalence point ($\text{CO}_3^{2-} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{HCO}_3^-$) is at 29 mL (the second, at 58 mL, is twice this). $n(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3) = n(\text{HCl to 1st equivalence}) = 0.1024 \times 0.0290 = 2.970 \times 10^{-3}$ mol. Aliquot volume $= \dfrac{36.98}{2.360} = 15.67$ mL. $c = \dfrac{2.970 \times 10^{-3}}{0.01567} = 0.1895$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
Consider the following reaction at 300 K.

$$2\text{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$$

Write the $K_{eq}$ expression for the reaction.
questions.answer: $$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{NO}]^2[\text{O}_2]}{[\text{NO}_2]^2}$$

questions.question:
Consider the following reaction at 300 K.

$$2\text{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$$

1.00 mol of NO$_2(g)$ is placed into a 2.00 L container and the system was allowed to reach equilibrium. At equilibrium, the concentration of NO$_2(g)$ was found to be 0.250 mol L$^{-1}$.

Calculate the equilibrium concentrations of NO$(g)$ and O$_2(g)$ at 300 K.

Consider the following reaction at 300 K.

$$2\text{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$$

1.00 mol of NO$_2(g)$ is placed into a 2.00 L container and the system was allowed to reach equilibrium. At equilibrium, the concentration of NO$_2(g)$ was found to be 0.250 mol L$^{-1}$.

Using the equilibrium concentrations $[\text{NO}] = 0.250$ mol L$^{-1}$ and $[\text{O}_2] = 0.125$ mol L$^{-1}$, calculate the equilibrium constant, $K_{eq}$, at this temperature.
questions.answer:
$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{NO}]^2[\text{O}_2]}{[\text{NO}_2]^2} = \frac{(0.250)^2(0.125)}{(0.250)^2} = 0.125$$

(3 significant figures, matching the data.)

questions.question:
Propene readily undergoes hydration (H$^+$/H$_2$O) to produce a mixture of two products, **A** and **B**. Compound **B** is propan-2-ol, CH$_3$CH(OH)CH$_3$. When separated, **A** and **B** are each oxidised with acidified dichromate (H$^+$/Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$, heat under reflux) to produce **C** and **D** respectively, where **D** is propanone (shown in the reaction scheme).

Draw the structures of **A** and **C**, and state the names of **A**, **B**, **C** and **D**.
questions.answer:
**A**: CH$_3$CH$_2$CH$_2$OH (the OH on the end carbon) — **propan-1-ol**

**B**: CH$_3$CH(OH)CH$_3$ — **propan-2-ol**

**C**: CH$_3$CH$_2$COOH (a carboxyl group, C(=O)–OH, on the end carbon) — **propanoic acid** (a primary alcohol is oxidised to the carboxylic acid under reflux)

**D**: CH$_3$COCH$_3$ — **propanone** (a secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone)

questions.question: Propan-2-ol (CH$_3$CH(OH)CH$_3$) has a boiling point of 82 °C and propanone (CH$_3$COCH$_3$) has a boiling point of 56 °C. Explain why propan-2-ol has a higher boiling point than propanone.
questions.answer:
Propan-2-ol contains a hydroxyl (–OH) group, so its strongest intermolecular force is **hydrogen bonding** between the H of one molecule's O–H and a lone pair on the O of a neighbouring molecule. Propanone has a carbonyl (C=O) group but no H bonded to O, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself; its strongest intermolecular forces are **dipole–dipole forces** between the polar C=O groups (plus dispersion forces, which are similar for the two molecules of similar size).

Hydrogen bonds are stronger than dipole–dipole forces, so **more energy is required to separate** propan-2-ol molecules into the gas phase. Therefore propan-2-ol has the higher boiling point.

questions.question:
Two pieces of cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated ammonia were placed at opposite ends of a glass tube. After some time, the solutions vaporise, and the two gases react to produce a ring of white powder.

Write an equation for the reaction that occurs inside the glass tube.
questions.answer: $$\text{HCl}(g) + \text{NH}_3(g) \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$$

questions.question:
Two pieces of cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated ammonia were placed at opposite ends of a glass tube. After some time, the solutions vaporise, and the two gases react to produce a ring of white powder.

The reaction is $\text{HCl}(g) + \text{NH}_3(g) \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$. State which acid–base theory explains the behaviour in this reaction and justify your answer.
questions.answer: The **Brønsted–Lowry theory**. The reaction occurs in the gas phase with no water present, so the Arrhenius theory (which needs H$^+$/OH$^-$ ions in aqueous solution) cannot describe it. In Brønsted–Lowry terms, HCl acts as an acid because it **donates a proton** (H$^+$) and NH$_3$ acts as a base because it **accepts the proton**, forming NH$_4^+$ (and Cl$^-$), which make up the ionic solid NH$_4$Cl.

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium reaction:

$$\text{CH}_4(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g)$$

Use collision theory to explain how a decrease in volume would affect the rates of the forward and reverse reactions initially and until equilibrium is re-established.
questions.answer:
Decreasing the volume increases the concentration (partial pressure) of every gas in the mixture. Particles collide more frequently, so the frequency of successful collisions increases for both reactants and products: **both the forward and reverse rates increase immediately**.

The reverse reaction involves 4 mol of gas particles (CO + 3H$_2$) colliding, compared with 2 mol (CH$_4$ + H$_2$O) for the forward reaction, so the increase in concentration increases the frequency of successful collisions for the reverse reaction relatively more. Initially, therefore, **the reverse rate increases more than the forward rate** (reverse rate > forward rate), and the system shifts to the left.

As the reverse reaction proceeds, [CO] and [H$_2$] decrease, so **the reverse rate gradually decreases**, while [CH$_4$] and [H$_2$O] increase, so **the forward rate gradually increases**.

When the two rates become equal again, equilibrium is re-established. **At the new equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, and both are faster than at the original equilibrium** because all concentrations are higher in the smaller volume.

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium reaction:

$$\text{CH}_4(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g)$$

Describe how the addition of a catalyst would affect the rates of the forward and reverse reactions and the position of the equilibrium.
questions.answer: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful in both directions. **The forward and reverse rates increase by the same factor** (equally), so equilibrium is reached faster, but **the position of equilibrium (and $K_{eq}$) is unchanged** — the equilibrium concentrations stay the same.

questions.question:
Alcohols can undergo elimination and substitution reactions under different conditions. A sample of 2-methylbutan-2-ol was subjected to an experimental set of conditions to determine whether elimination (giving 2-methylbut-2-ene) or substitution (giving 2-chloro-2-methylbutane) would occur.

The sole product of the reaction was purified and analysed using $^{13}$C NMR spectroscopy. The $^{13}$C NMR spectrum is shown below.

Deduce which of the two possible products was formed in the reaction. Explain your choice using $^{13}$C NMR data.
questions.answer:
The product is **2-methylbut-2-ene** (the elimination product).

The spectrum has two peaks well above 100 ppm (at about 118 and 132 ppm). According to the $^{13}$C NMR data sheet, shifts of about 90–150 ppm correspond to carbons in a C=C double bond, so the product contains an alkene. 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane has no C=C; its most deshielded carbon (the C–Cl carbon) would appear at about 70 ppm, so it would give no signal above 100 ppm.

*Note: the original solutions quote the alkene peaks as about 138 and 163 ppm; the spectrum shows them at about 118 and 132 ppm, within the C=C range.*

questions.question:
The graph shows the trend in standard enthalpy of combustion values (reported as $-\Delta_c H^\ominus$) for the first five alkanes (methane to pentane), in kJ mol$^{-1}$.

Explain the trend observed.
questions.answer:
As the number of carbon atoms in the alkane increases, the enthalpy of combustion ($-\Delta_c H^\ominus$) increases in a regular (approximately linear) way, by about 650 kJ mol$^{-1}$ per carbon — i.e. more heat is released per mole of alkane burned.

Each successive alkane differs by a –CH$_2$– unit. Combustion of each extra CH$_2$ unit requires breaking more C–C and C–H bonds (and O=O bonds), which is endothermic, but it also forms one extra CO$_2$ and one extra H$_2$O, and forming the strong C=O and O–H bonds in these products is exothermic.

Because the energy released in forming the bonds in the extra products is greater than the energy absorbed in breaking the extra bonds in the reactants, each additional CH$_2$ unit adds a roughly constant net amount of energy released, so more energy is released per mole of alkane combusted as the chain gets longer.

questions.question:
The graph shows the trend in standard enthalpy of combustion values (reported as $-\Delta_c H^\ominus$) for the first five alkanes (methane to pentane), in kJ mol$^{-1}$.

Using the graph, calculate the energy released from the combustion of pentane, in kJ g$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
From the graph, for pentane (5 carbons) $-\Delta_c H^\ominus = 3500$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

$M(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}) = 5(12.01) + 12(1.008) = 72.146$ g mol$^{-1}$

Energy released per gram $= \dfrac{3500}{72.146} = 48.5$ kJ g$^{-1}$

questions.question:
A beaker contains 105 mL of saturated calcium sulfate solution at 25 °C. The $K_{sp}$ for CaSO$_4$ is $4.93 \times 10^{-5}$ at 25 °C.

Calculate the molar solubility of calcium sulfate in water at this temperature.
questions.answer:
$\text{CaSO}_4(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ca}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)$

Let $s$ = molar solubility, so $[\text{Ca}^{2+}] = [\text{SO}_4^{2-}] = s$.

$K_{sp} = s^2 = 4.93 \times 10^{-5} \Rightarrow s = \sqrt{4.93 \times 10^{-5}} = 7.02 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$

questions.question:
A beaker contains 105 mL of saturated calcium sulfate solution at 25 °C. The $K_{sp}$ for CaSO$_4$ is $4.93 \times 10^{-5}$ at 25 °C, so its molar solubility is $7.02 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

145 mL of 0.500 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium sulfate solution is added to the saturated calcium sulfate. Determine whether a precipitate will form and justify your answer with calculations.

The following reactions are performed at 823 K.

Reaction 1: $\text{CoO}(s) + \text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Co}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \qquad K_{eq1} = 67$

Reaction 2: $\text{CoO}(s) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Co}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) \qquad K_{eq2} = 490$

Use the information provided to calculate the value for the equilibrium constant, $K_{eq3}$, at 823 K for Reaction 3. Show your working.

Reaction 3: $\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \qquad K_{eq3} = ?$
questions.answer:
Reverse reaction 2 (which inverts its constant):

$\text{Co}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CoO}(s) + \text{CO}(g) \qquad K = \dfrac{1}{490}$

Add it to reaction 1 (adding equations multiplies the constants); CoO and Co cancel:

$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$

$$K_{eq3} = K_{eq1} \times \frac{1}{K_{eq2}} = \frac{67}{490} = 0.137 \;(0.14)$$

Check: $K_{eq1} = \dfrac{[\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{H}_2]}$, $K_{eq2} = \dfrac{[\text{CO}_2]}{[\text{CO}]}$, so $\dfrac{K_{eq1}}{K_{eq2}} = \dfrac{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{H}_2][\text{CO}_2]} = K_{eq3}$.

questions.question:
For the reaction

$$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$$

the equilibrium constant is $K_{eq} = 0.137$ at 823 K. At 1973 K the value of $K_{eq}$ is 4.9. Justify whether the forward reaction is endothermic or exothermic.
questions.answer:
$K_{eq} = \dfrac{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{H}_2][\text{CO}_2]}$ increases from 0.137 to 4.9 as the temperature increases from 823 K to 1973 K, so at higher temperature the equilibrium lies further to the right (more products).

By Le Chatelier's principle, increasing the temperature shifts an equilibrium in the direction that absorbs heat (the endothermic direction) to oppose the change. Since the forward reaction is favoured at higher temperature, **the forward reaction is endothermic**.

questions.question: Outline how infrared spectroscopy could be used to distinguish between a sample of cyclohexanone and a sample of cyclohexanol.
questions.answer:
Cyclohexanol contains an alcohol O–H group, so its IR spectrum will show a strong, **broad absorption at 3230–3550 cm$^{-1}$**; cyclohexanone has no O–H, so this absorption is absent.

Cyclohexanone contains a C=O group, so its spectrum will show a strong, **sharp absorption at 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$**; this is absent from the cyclohexanol spectrum.

questions.question: Samples of cyclohexane (C$_6$H$_{12}$) and bromocyclohexane (C$_6$H$_{11}$Br) cannot be easily distinguished from one another using infrared spectroscopy. Suggest another analytical technique that can be used to distinguish the two and refer to any differences in the spectra.
questions.answer:
**Mass spectrometry.** Cyclohexane gives a molecular ion peak at $m/z = 84$. Bromocyclohexane gives two molecular ion peaks of approximately equal height at $m/z = 162$ and $164$, because bromine exists as two isotopes, $^{79}$Br and $^{81}$Br, in about a 1 : 1 ratio.

(Alternatively, **$^{13}$C NMR**: cyclohexane has only 1 carbon environment, so 1 peak, whereas bromocyclohexane has 4 carbon environments (C1, C2/C6, C3/C5, C4), so 4 peaks, including one shifted downfield by the C–Br.)

questions.question: Calculate the volume of water that must be added to a 220.0 mL solution of sodium hydroxide with a pH of 13.030 to achieve a solution with a final pH of 12.699 at 25 °C.

The structure of a cationic detergent, cetrimonium (a long hydrocarbon chain bonded to a positively charged trimethylammonium group, $-\text{N}^+(\text{CH}_3)_3$), is shown.

With reference to its structure, explain how cetrimonium can be used to produce a stable emulsion of oil in water.
questions.answer:
Cetrimonium has two distinct regions. The long hydrocarbon chain (16 carbons) is non-polar and **hydrophobic**; the $-\text{N}^+(\text{CH}_3)_3$ head is ionic (positively charged) and **hydrophilic**.

When the detergent is shaken with oil and water, the hydrophobic tails dissolve in the oil droplets, interacting with the non-polar oil molecules through dispersion forces. The charged heads stay at the droplet surface, projecting into the water, where they form **ion–dipole forces** with polar water molecules.

In this way the oil is broken up into tiny droplets, each surrounded by detergent molecules — a **micelle** with the oil inside and a layer of positive charges on the outside.

Because every droplet's surface is positively charged, neighbouring droplets **repel each other** and cannot coalesce into a separate oil layer, while the hydrophilic heads keep the droplets dispersed in the water. The result is a stable emulsion of oil in water.

questions.question:
Hypochlorous acid, HOCl, is a sterilising agent used in swimming pools. It is produced when chlorine reacts with water according to the equation shown.

$$\text{Cl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{HCl}(aq)$$

HOCl ionises to form the hypochlorite ion, OCl$^-$, which is a less effective disinfectant than the undissociated acid. The graph shows the concentrations of HOCl$(aq)$ and OCl$^-(aq)$ at different pH values at 25 °C.

Deduce the pH range where the water is most effectively sterilised.
questions.answer: Between about **pH 0 and pH 6**: in this range essentially 100% of the chlorine is present as undissociated HOCl, the more effective disinfectant (above pH 6, HOCl ionises to the less effective OCl$^-$).

questions.question:
Hypochlorous acid, HOCl, is a sterilising agent used in swimming pools. It is produced when chlorine reacts with water according to the equation shown.

$$\text{Cl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{HCl}(aq)$$

HOCl ionises to form the hypochlorite ion, OCl$^-$, which is a less effective disinfectant than the undissociated acid. The graph shows the concentrations of HOCl$(aq)$ and OCl$^-(aq)$ at different pH values at 25 °C.

With reference to the graph, determine the p$K_a$ of HOCl at 25 °C.
questions.answer: p$K_a$ is the pH at which $[\text{HOCl}] = [\text{OCl}^-]$ (50% each), i.e. where the two curves cross: **p$K_a \approx 7.5$** (any value from 7.3 to 7.7).

questions.question: Hypochlorous acid, HOCl, is a weak acid with p$K_a = 7.5$ at 25 °C. Calculate the pH of 0.100 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOCl at 25 °C.
questions.answer:
OCl$^-$ is the conjugate base of HOCl: p$K_b = 14 - 7.5 = 6.5$, so $K_b = 10^{-6.5} = 3.16 \times 10^{-7}$.

$\text{OCl}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)$

| | OCl$^-$ | HOCl | OH$^-$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0.100 | 0 | 0 |
| Change | $-x$ | $+x$ | $+x$ |
| Equilibrium | $0.100 - x$ | $x$ | $x$ |

$K_b = \dfrac{[\text{HOCl}][\text{OH}^-]}{[\text{OCl}^-]} = \dfrac{x^2}{0.100 - x} \approx \dfrac{x^2}{0.100}$ (assuming $x \ll 0.100$)

$x^2 = 3.16 \times 10^{-8} \Rightarrow x = [\text{OH}^-] = 1.78 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$ (assumption valid: $x$ is 0.18% of 0.100)

pOH $= -\log_{10}(1.78 \times 10^{-4}) = 3.75$, so **pH $= 14 - 3.75 = 10.25$**

questions.question:
A new brand of orange juice claims to contain at least 300.0 mg of vitamin C, C$_6$H$_8$O$_6$, per 100 mL serving size on its label. A back titration involving iodine was performed to test this claim.

Iodine was produced by adding 10.93 mL of 0.001025 mol L$^{-1}$ aqueous potassium iodate, KIO$_3(aq)$, to an excess of aqueous potassium iodide solution.

$$\text{KIO}_3(aq) + 6\text{H}^+(aq) + 5\text{I}^-(aq) \rightarrow 3\text{I}_2(aq) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{K}^+(aq)$$

A 100.0 mL sample of the commercial orange juice was then diluted to 1.000 L using deionised water. A 25.00 mL aliquot of the diluted orange juice was then added to the iodine produced.

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_6(aq) + \text{I}_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}_6(aq) + 2\text{I}^-(aq) + 2\text{H}^+(aq)$$

The excess iodine was then titrated against 0.001135 mol L$^{-1}$ thiosulfate solution as shown.

$$\text{I}_2(aq) + 2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}(aq) + 2\text{I}^-(aq)$$

The experiment was repeated, and the results are shown below.

| Trial | Volume of Na$_2$S$_2$O$_3$ added (mL) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 19.80 |
| 2 | 12.25 |
| 3 | 12.35 |
| 4 | 12.30 |

Assess the accuracy of the claim made on the label of the orange juice and show your working. The $MM$ of vitamin C is 176.124 g mol$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
Trial 1 is an outlier (rough titre), so average the concordant titres: $\bar{V} = \dfrac{12.25 + 12.35 + 12.30}{3} = 12.30$ mL

$n(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}) = 0.001135 \times 0.01230 = 1.396 \times 10^{-5}$ mol

$n(\text{I}_2 \text{ in excess}) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.396 \times 10^{-5} = 6.980 \times 10^{-6}$ mol

$n(\text{I}_2 \text{ produced}) = 3 \times n(\text{KIO}_3) = 3 \times 0.001025 \times 0.01093 = 3.361 \times 10^{-5}$ mol

$n(\text{I}_2 \text{ reacted with vitamin C}) = 3.361 \times 10^{-5} - 6.980 \times 10^{-6} = 2.663 \times 10^{-5}$ mol

$n(\text{vitamin C in 25.00 mL aliquot}) = 2.663 \times 10^{-5}$ mol (1 : 1)

The 100.0 mL juice sample was diluted to 1.000 L, and 25.00 mL of that was used, so the 100 mL serving contains $\dfrac{1000}{25.00} = 40$ times the aliquot:

$n(\text{vitamin C per 100 mL}) = 40 \times 2.663 \times 10^{-5} = 1.065 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$m = 1.065 \times 10^{-3} \times 176.124 = 0.1876$ g $= 187.6$ mg per 100 mL

187.6 mg is well below the claimed minimum of 300.0 mg per 100 mL, so **the claim on the label is not accurate** (the juice contains only about 63% of the claimed amount).

questions.question:
The enthalpy of solution is described by the following equation:

$$\Delta H_{sol}^\ominus = \Delta H_{latt}^\ominus + \Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus$$

Values for the lattice enthalpy ($\Delta H_{latt}^\ominus$), hydration enthalpy ($\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus$) and entropy of solution ($\Delta S_{sol}^\ominus$) have been given for two ionic compounds, lead(II) chloride and lead(II) iodide.

| Compound | $\Delta H_{latt}^\ominus$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | $\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | $\Delta S_{sol}^\ominus$ (J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| PbCl$_2$ | $+683$ | $-1820$ | $+136.0$ |
| PbI$_2$ | $+591$ | $-1540$ | $+174.9$ |

State which of the two lead(II) salts is the more soluble and use all values in the table to explain this difference in solubility of lead(II) chloride and lead(II) iodide in water. (You do not need to calculate $\Delta G$ to answer this question.)
questions.answer:
**Lead(II) chloride is the more soluble salt.**

Breaking up the lattice is endothermic ($\Delta H_{latt} > 0$) and hydrating the ions is exothermic ($\Delta H_{hyd} < 0$):

$\Delta H_{sol}(\text{PbCl}_2) = +683 - 1820 = -1137$ kJ mol$^{-1}$

$\Delta H_{sol}(\text{PbI}_2) = +591 - 1540 = -949$ kJ mol$^{-1}$

Although more energy is needed to break the PbCl$_2$ lattice (the smaller Cl$^-$ ions are held more strongly), much more energy is released when its ions are hydrated (the smaller Cl$^-$ ion attracts water molecules more strongly). So dissolving PbCl$_2$ is about 188 kJ mol$^{-1}$ more exothermic, which favours the dissolution of PbCl$_2$ more than that of PbI$_2$.

Both salts have a positive entropy of solution (the ordered lattice becomes dispersed, mobile ions), which favours dissolving. The entropy increase is larger for PbI$_2$ (+174.9 vs +136.0 J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$), so entropy favours PbI$_2$ slightly more.

However, the entropy difference is small: at 298 K it contributes only about $T\Delta S = 298 \times (0.1749 - 0.1360) \approx 12$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ in favour of PbI$_2$, much less than the 188 kJ mol$^{-1}$ enthalpy difference in favour of PbCl$_2$. The enthalpy factor therefore dominates, $\Delta G_{sol}$ is more negative for PbCl$_2$, and PbCl$_2$ is the more soluble salt (consistent with its larger $K_{sp}$, $1.70 \times 10^{-5}$ vs $9.8 \times 10^{-9}$ for PbI$_2$).

questions.question: Safranal (shown below) is a compound that naturally occurs in saffron. Identify two different functional groups found in safranal.
questions.answer:
Safranal contains:

- an **aldehyde** group (–CHO, the C=O with an H attached to the ring carbon), and
- **alkene** groups (the two C=C double bonds in the ring).

(Note: \"carbonyl\" alone is not enough — the carbonyl is part of an aldehyde functional group here.)

questions.question:
Safranal (shown first) can be converted into the compound shown second, 2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid, in two steps.

Describe how you could produce this compound from safranal, stating the reagents and conditions required for each step, and draw (or describe the structure of) the intermediate compound.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — hydrogenation (addition of H$_2$):** react safranal with hydrogen gas, H$_2(g)$, with a palladium (Pd/C) or platinum catalyst, with heat. Both ring C=C double bonds become single bonds.

Intermediate: **2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde** — a saturated cyclohexane ring carrying the –CHO group on C1, two methyl groups on C2 and one methyl group on C6 (the same skeleton as the product, with –CHO in place of –COOH).

**Step 2 — oxidation:** heat the intermediate under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate (H$^+$/Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$) or acidified potassium permanganate. The aldehyde group is oxidised to a carboxylic acid group, giving the product.

(The steps may also be done in the reverse order: oxidise the aldehyde first with acidified dichromate, giving 2,6,6-trimethylcyclohexa-1,3-diene-1-carboxylic acid as the intermediate, then hydrogenate the C=C bonds.)

questions.question:
What mass of solid sodium hydroxide should be added to 100.0 mL of 0.500 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl to increase the temperature by 5.00 °C?

You can assume that the specific heat capacity of the solution is $4.18 \times 10^{3}$ J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ (and that 100.0 mL of solution has a mass of 100.0 g).

$$\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \qquad \Delta H = -56.1\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
$$\text{NaOH}(s) \rightarrow \text{NaOH}(aq) \qquad \Delta H = -44.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
questions.answer:
**Step 1** (Hess's law): adding the two equations, $\text{NaOH}(s) + \text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ has $\Delta H = -56.1 + (-44.5) = -100.6$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

**Step 2**: $q = mc\Delta T = 0.1000\ \text{kg} \times 4.18 \times 10^3 \times 5.00 = 2090$ J $= 2.090$ kJ

**Step 3**: $n(\text{NaOH}) = \dfrac{q}{|\Delta H|} = \dfrac{2.090}{100.6} = 0.02078$ mol (less than the 0.0500 mol of HCl present, so all of it reacts)

**Step 4**: $m(\text{NaOH}) = 0.02078 \times 39.998 = 0.831$ g

(Including the mass of the dissolved NaOH and/or HCl in the mass of the solution gives 0.838–0.853 g, which is also acceptable.)

questions.question:
Compounds **X**, **Y** and **Z** are isomers containing 68.1% carbon, 13.7% hydrogen and 18.2% oxygen by mass. They have a molar mass of less than 100 g mol$^{-1}$.

A student performs chemical tests on the three compounds. Results of the tests are shown in the table below.

| Compound | Addition of oxidant, acidified potassium dichromate solution | Addition of Lucas reagent (conc. HCl$(aq)$ and ZnCl$_2(aq)$) |
|---|---|---|
| X | Orange solution remains | Precipitate forms immediately |
| Y | Orange solution turns green | Colourless solution remains |
| Z | Orange solution turns green | Precipitate forms after 5 minutes |

$^{1}$H NMR data is also given for compounds **X**, **Y** and **Z**:

| Compound X: shift (ppm) | Peak area ratio | Splitting |
|---|---|---|
| 0.99 | 3 | triplet |
| 1.20 | 1 | singlet |
| 1.30 | 6 | singlet |
| 1.53 | 2 | quartet |

| Compound Y: shift (ppm) | Peak area ratio | Splitting |
|---|---|---|
| 0.99 | 3 | triplet |
| 1.12 | 1 | singlet |
| 1.30 | 2 | multiplet |
| 1.37 | 2 | multiplet |
| 1.51 | 2 | multiplet |
| 3.57 | 2 | triplet |

| Compound Z: shift (ppm) | Peak area ratio | Splitting |
|---|---|---|
| 1.01 | 6 | doublet |
| 1.10 | 1 | singlet |
| 1.25 | 3 | doublet |
| 1.49 | 1 | multiplet |
| 3.50 | 1 | multiplet |

$^{1}$H NMR chemical shift data: R–CH$_3$ 0.9–1.0; R–CH$_2$–R 1.2–1.5; R–CHR$_2$ 1.5–2.0; –CH$_2$–O– (alcohols, ethers or esters) 3.3–4.8; R–OH 1–6 ppm.

Draw and name compounds **X**, **Y** and **Z** and, by using all information given, justify your choice for compound **X**.
questions.answer:
**Molecular formula.** Mole ratio C : H : O $= \dfrac{68.1}{12.01} : \dfrac{13.7}{1.008} : \dfrac{18.2}{16.00} = 5.67 : 13.6 : 1.14 = 5 : 12 : 1$, so the empirical formula is C$_5$H$_{12}$O ($M = 88.15$ g mol$^{-1}$). The next multiple, C$_{10}$H$_{24}$O$_2$ (176.3 g mol$^{-1}$), exceeds 100 g mol$^{-1}$, so the molecular formula is **C$_5$H$_{12}$O**. Every NMR spectrum includes a 1H singlet in the 1–6 ppm O–H range and the compounds react with oxidant/Lucas reagent, so they are alcohols.

**X = 2-methylbutan-2-ol**, CH$_3$CH$_2$C(OH)(CH$_3$)$_2$ (a tertiary alcohol)

**Y = pentan-1-ol**, CH$_3$CH$_2$CH$_2$CH$_2$CH$_2$OH (a primary alcohol)

**Z = 3-methylbutan-2-ol**, CH$_3$CH(OH)CH(CH$_3$)$_2$ (a secondary alcohol)

**Justification for X.**

*Chemical tests:* X does not reduce acidified dichromate (stays orange), so it has no H on the C–OH carbon — it is not a primary or secondary alcohol. It reacts immediately with Lucas reagent (forming an insoluble chloroalkane), which is characteristic of a tertiary alcohol. (Y: oxidised but no Lucas reaction → primary; Z: oxidised and slow Lucas reaction → secondary.)

*$^1$H NMR:* four peaks show four H environments, with area ratio 3 : 1 : 6 : 2 = 12 H, matching C$_5$H$_{12}$O.

- 0.99 ppm, 3H, triplet: a CH$_3$ (R–CH$_3$, 0.9–1.0 ppm) next to a CH$_2$ (2 neighbouring H → $n + 1 = 3$) — the CH$_3$ of an ethyl group.
- 1.20 ppm, 1H, singlet: the O–H proton (R–OH, 1–6 ppm), not coupled.
- 1.30 ppm, 6H, singlet: two equivalent CH$_3$ groups on the same carbon; a singlet means that carbon has no H — it is the quaternary C–OH carbon, confirming a tertiary alcohol.
- 1.53 ppm, 2H, quartet: a CH$_2$ (R–CH$_2$–R) next to a CH$_3$ (3 neighbouring H → quartet), bonded on its other side to the quaternary carbon.

No peak appears at 3.3–4.8 ppm, confirming there is no H on the carbon bearing the OH. These data fit only (CH$_3$)$_2$C(OH)CH$_2$CH$_3$, 2-methylbutan-2-ol.
